name: Zero balancing

image.caption: Fulcrum into skeletal foot.zero balancing tutorial

lead: Zero balancing is a manual therapy created by osteopathic doctor Fritz Smith in the early 1970s. The client stays clothed while the practitioner applies gentle pressure and stretching, mostly at joints and bones.
People use it for relaxation and a sense of structural alignment. Any appearance benefit would be indirect, through posture and ease of movement; practitioners do not typically market it for looks.

paras: Sessions are usually short and done fully clothed on a table, using lifting, pressing and rotating touches around the skeleton.
The touch is gentle and risks are low. Researchers and critics, including Edzard Ernst, note that no efficacy evidence has been published.

angle.text: Practitioners describe it as improving how the body holds itself; any visible change would come through posture and relaxation.

lead: Zero balancing (ZB) is a manual therapy developed by osteopath Frederick 'Fritz' Smith in the early 1970s, combining Eastern ideas with Western bodywork.[1]
Practitioners say it balances body energy with body structure through conscious touch, working on the bones while the client is clothed.[1][2]

Within looksmaxxing-style interest it is only occasionally mentioned, as a possible route to relaxation and better posture. Edzard Ernst wrote in 2018 that published efficacy evidence appears absent.[1]

paras: Smith held that energy currents are stored in the skeleton and that imbalances in the field precede pathology.[1] Sessions use gentle lifting, pressing, rotating and stretching, with attention on bones.[1]

The Wikipedia article calls it pseudoscientific and cites Jann Bellamy's critique of vitalism-based bodywork regulation.[1] Proponents describe it in nursing-literature terms as a bridge between energetic and structural therapies.[2]
No studies found. Available literature consists of conceptual reviews and descriptions of the therapy.[3][2]
